# Community conservation, institutions, and participatory governance

::: {.lead}
I study how communities, states, and conservation organizations govern land and wildlife, with a focus on community-based natural resource management, social capital, and institutional change in Southern Africa.
:::

::: {.bio-text}
My work sits at the intersection of political ecology, social-ecological systems, and institutional analysis. I am especially interested in how incomplete devolution of authority and proprietorship rights shapes the capacity of community-based conservation to deliver conservation, livelihoods, and democratic governance outcomes.

I combine household surveys, field interviews, participatory methods, governance audits, GIS, and spatial statistics. Much of this work is collaborative and community-facing: survey findings are returned to communities and practitioners to support adaptive management, participatory budgeting, and more inclusive decision-making.
:::

## Research at a glance

::: {.site-note}
Current work links institutional design, social trust, participation, and spatial variation in community conservation governance.
:::
:::

::: {.card-grid}
::: {.site-card}
<span class="card-label">Institutions</span>

### Devolution and authority

I examine CBNRM as an institutional development process, asking how partial or “aborted” devolution shapes conservation and rural development.
:::

::: {.site-card}
<span class="card-label">Participation</span>

### Governance and social capital

My empirical work analyzes who participates in conservation governance, where participation clusters spatially, and how trust and fairness shape inclusion.
:::

::: {.site-card}
<span class="card-label">Methods</span>

### Surveys, GIS, and fieldwork

I use mixed methods, household survey data, spatial statistics, institutional audits, interviews, and participatory research tools.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.split-feature}
::: {.split-copy}
## Current work

My dissertation, *Institutions, Authority, and Governance: Understanding the Performance of Community-Based Natural Resource Management in Southern Africa*, investigates why CBNRM has generated important conservation gains while delivering more uneven outcomes in livelihoods, development, and political empowerment.

The project combines comparative institutional analysis with original household survey data from six communal conservancies in Namibia.

## Teaching and mentorship

I teach human-environment geography through applied, student-centered learning. My courses emphasize real data, spatial thinking, and the relationship between environmental change, political economy, institutions, and inequality.

I am prepared to teach environmental governance, political ecology, environmental justice, economic geography, GIS, mixed methods, and community-based conservation.
:::
:::

::: {.site-card}
